stem: A cancer survivor says, 'My follow-up scan is next week. I am so afraid the cancer is back that I am thinking about canceling the appointment.' Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: Acknowledge the fear, assess how much it is affecting sleep, daily function, and follow-up care, encourage the client to keep the recommended follow-up plan, and offer psychosocial support or counseling if needed.
options.B: Tell the client there is no reason to worry because completing treatment guarantees that the cancer will not recur.
options.C: Support canceling the scan because avoiding cancer-related reminders is the best way to reduce fear of recurrence.
options.D: Explain that fear of recurrence is abnormal after treatment and indicates that the client has a psychiatric disorder.

rationale: Fear of cancer recurrence is common after treatment and often intensifies around follow-up visits, scans, and test results. NCI advises survivors to discuss these fears with the healthcare team, follow the recommended survivorship plan, and seek counseling when fear becomes difficult to manage. The nurse should assess the severity and functional impact of the anxiety and support continued follow-up rather than encouraging avoidance. Reassuring the client that recurrence is impossible is inaccurate, while labeling all recurrence fear as psychiatric illness fails to distinguish common worry from clinically significant distress.
educational_objective: Respond to fear of cancer recurrence by validating the concern, assessing its impact, supporting recommended follow-up care, and facilitating psychosocial help when anxiety becomes difficult to manage.

correction_summary: Rebuilt the original definition-only fear-of-recurrence item into an applied survivorship scenario in which anxiety is beginning to interfere with recommended follow-up care. The final response validates the common concern, assesses functional impact, protects continuity of surveillance, and offers counseling without falsely guaranteeing cure or pathologizing normal survivorship anxiety.
audit_findings: Original item tested only recognition that fear of recurrence is common and used weak, obviously incorrect distractors.
Fresh NCI survivorship guidance directly supports scan-related anxiety, discussion with the healthcare team, continued follow-up, and counseling when fear is difficult to manage.
The final item distinguishes common recurrence fear from clinically significant distress by assessing functional impact rather than automatically assigning a psychiatric diagnosis.
The response avoids false reassurance and protects adherence to individualized survivorship surveillance.
Independent adversarial review found one uniquely correct therapeutic response with no ambiguity, second answer, cueing, unsupported recurrence guarantee, or unresolved source conflict.
